name: Genome Nexus
description: We require a system, Genome Nexus, to serve as a comprehensive, centralized resource for the rapid, automated, and high-throughput annotation and interpretation of genetic variants in cancer. This system needs to integrate information from a variety of existing databases. Its primary function will be to provide insights by converting DNA changes to protein changes, predicting the functional effects of protein mutations, and offering data on mutation frequencies, gene function, variant effects, and clinical actionability. The system should also be capable of supporting analysis for different species, including human and mouse.
rawDescription:
# Genome Nexus 🧬

Genome Nexus, a comprehensive one-stop resource for fast, automated and
high-throughput annotation and interpretation of genetic variants in cancer.
Genome Nexus integrates information from a variety of existing resources,
including databases that convert DNA changes to protein changes, predict the
functional effects of protein mutations, and contain information about mutation
frequencies, gene function, variant effects, and clinical actionability.

## Documentation 📖
See the [docs](https://docs.genomenexus.org)

## Run 💻

### Alternative 1 - run genome-nexus, mongoDB and genome-nexus-vep in docker containers
First, set environment variables for Ensembl Release, VEP Assembly, location of VEP Cache, and species (since a mouse instalation is supported). If these are not, the default values from `.env` will be set.

The reference genome and Ensembl release must be consistent with a version in [genome-nexus-importer/data/](https://github.com/genome-nexus/genome-nexus-importer/tree/master/data).
For example `grch37_ensembl92`, `grch38_ensembl92` or `grch38_ensembl95`:
```
export REF_ENSEMBL_VERSION=grch38_ensembl92
```
If you want to setup Genome Nexus for mouse, also set the `SPECIES` variable to 'mus_musculus'. Also see the [docs](https://github.com/genome-nexus/genome-nexus-importer/blob/master/docs/setup-genome-nexus-mouse.md) to create a mouse database.
```bash
export SPECIES=mus_musculus
```

If you would like to do local VEP annotations instead of using the public Ensembl API, please uncomment `# gn_vep.region.url=http://localhost:6060/vep/human/region/VARIANT` in your `application.properties`. This will require you to download the VEP cache files for the preferred Ensembl Release and Reference genome, see our documentation on [downloading the Genome Nexus VEP Cache](https://github.com/genome-nexus/genome-nexus-vep/blob/master/README.md#create-vep-cache). This will take several hours.
```
# Set local cache dir
export VEP_CACHE=<local_vep_cache>

# GRCh38 or GRCh37
export VEP_ASSEMBLY=GRCh38
```

Run docker-compose to create images and containers:
```
docker-compose up --build -d
```

Run without recreating images:
```
docker-compose up -d
```

Run without Genome Nexus VEP:
```
# Start both the Web and DB (dependency of Web) containers
docker-compose up -d web
```

Stop and remove containers:
```
docker-compose down
```

### Alternative 2 - run genome-nexus locally, but mongoDB in docker container
```
# the genomenexus/gn-mongo images comes with all the required tables imported
# change latest to different version if necessary (only need to run this once)
docker run --name=gn-mongo --restart=always -p 27017:27017 -d genomenexus/gn-mongo:latest 
mvn  -DskipTests clean install
java -jar web/target/web-*.war
```

### Alternative 3 - install mongoDB locally and run with local java
Install mongoDB manually. Then follow instructions in
[genome-nexus-importer](https://github.com/genome-nexus/genome-nexus-importer)
to initialize the database.

After that run this:
```
mvn clean install
java -jar web/target/web-*.war
```

highLevelGoals: The Cancer Researcher aims to utilize the system for in-depth annotation and interpretation of genetic variants, facilitating a deeper understanding of their role in cancer biology.
The Cancer Researcher seeks to access comprehensive data on gene function and the effects of mutations to advance their research into cancer mechanisms.
The Cancer Researcher desires to analyze mutation frequencies and patterns to identify significant trends and insights relevant to cancer development and progression.
The Clinical Oncologist aims to gain critical insights into genetic variants and their functional effects to accurately diagnose cancer patients.
The Clinical Oncologist seeks to access data on the clinical actionability of genetic variants to make evidence-based and personalized treatment decisions for patients.
The Clinical Oncologist desires to understand the predicted functional effects of protein mutations to better anticipate and manage patient outcomes.
The Bioinformatician aims to leverage the system for efficient, automated, and high-throughput annotation of genetic variants.
The Bioinformatician seeks to integrate information from various existing databases to perform comprehensive and complex analysis of genomic variants.
The Bioinformatician requires the system to support the analysis of genomic variants across different species, including human and mouse, for comparative studies.
The Bioinformatician desires the system to automatically convert DNA changes to protein changes and predict their functional effects, streamlining analytical workflows.
lowLevelGoals: Allows the Cancer Researcher to input a specific genetic variant ID and receive comprehensive annotation data, including genomic location, gene context, and known associations.
Enables the Cancer Researcher to search for existing interpretations and clinical significance of a genetic variant specifically within the context of cancer.
Provides the Cancer Researcher with the ability to narrow down variant searches by selecting specific cancer types, focusing on relevant variants.
Allows the Cancer Researcher to obtain detailed functional information for a given gene, including its pathways, protein domains, and known biological roles.
Enables the Cancer Researcher to input a mutation and receive predictions on its potential impact on the function of the affected protein.
Provides the Cancer Researcher with access to published experimental data and studies that validate or describe the functional consequences of a specific mutation.
Allows the Cancer Researcher to search for and obtain statistical data on how often a particular mutation appears in various cancer patient populations.
Enables the Cancer Researcher to generate graphical representations of mutation distribution and hotspots within a chosen gene or genomic segment.
Provides the Cancer Researcher with data and analyses on whether certain mutations tend to appear together in the same cancer samples, indicating potential synergistic effects.
Allows the Clinical Oncologist to upload or input a patient's genetic variant information and receive system-generated insights relevant to cancer diagnosis.
Enables the Clinical Oncologist to search for established links between a particular genetic variant and specific cancer diseases or syndromes.
Provides the Clinical Oncologist with a concise overview of how a genetic variant's functional effects contribute to or are relevant for a cancer diagnosis.
Allows the Clinical Oncologist to obtain a curated list of genetic variants that have known clinical implications and can guide treatment decisions for a specified cancer type.
Enables the Clinical Oncologist to search for specific drug therapies or treatment strategies that are recommended or contraindicated based on the presence of a particular genetic variant.
Provides the Clinical Oncologist with data indicating whether a specific genetic variant makes a patient more or less likely to respond to certain cancer drugs.
Allows the Clinical Oncologist to obtain information on how a particular genetic variant might influence a patient's disease course, recurrence risk, or overall survival.
Provides the Clinical Oncologist with statistical data and Kaplan-Meier curves showing survival rates for patient cohorts grouped by the presence or absence of specific genetic variants.
Enables the Clinical Oncologist to analyze and compare the effectiveness of various treatment approaches in patients who share a common genetic variant.
Allows the Bioinformatician to upload a file containing multiple genetic variants (e.g., VCF) for high-throughput, automated processing and annotation by the system.
Enables the Bioinformatician to customize the settings and parameters of the variant annotation workflow, such as choosing specific databases or prediction algorithms.
Provides the Bioinformatician with real-time updates on the progress and completion status of their batch variant annotation tasks.
Allows the Bioinformatician to export the results of variant annotation in various standard file formats suitable for further analysis.
Enables the Bioinformatician to select and integrate data from various public and proprietary genomic databases during the annotation process.
Allows the Bioinformatician to search for a specific variant and receive a consolidated view of its information pulled from all integrated databases.
Provides the Bioinformatician with the capability to import their own experimental or proprietary genomic data to be analyzed alongside the system's existing datasets.
Enables the Bioinformatician to specify the organism for which variant annotation and analysis should be performed, supporting multi-species studies.
Allows the Bioinformatician to identify and retrieve corresponding genes (orthologs) in different species for comparative genomic studies.
Enables the Bioinformatician to compare the predicted or known functional effects of genetic variants in human and mouse models.
Allows the Bioinformatician to input genomic coordinates of a DNA variant and receive an automated prediction of the resulting amino acid change in the protein.
Enables the Bioinformatician to obtain automated predictions on whether a specific protein mutation is likely to be harmful, benign, or have other functional consequences.
Provides the Bioinformatician with control over which computational algorithms (e.g., SIFT, PolyPhen-2) are used by the system to predict the functional impact of variants.

baselineCritiques.actors: The identified actors (Cancer Researcher, Clinical Oncologist, Bioinformatician) are highly relevant and accurately reflect the primary user base for a system like Genome Nexus, which serves both research and clinical purposes. The descriptions align well with the system's capabilities (annotation, interpretation, clinical actionability, high-throughput analysis). There are no obvious contradictions or critical omissions regarding the main stakeholders. While one could argue for a "System Administrator" or "Database Curator" role, in the context of end-user roles for a resource platform, the current list is comprehensive and representative of the system's value proposition.
